title: ANALYZING SERVERS AND GETTING SUPPORT
display: Ch 16 — ANALYZING SERVERS AND GETTING SUPPORT

content.text: Book reference: Chapter 16, pages 557–597. Guided Exercises: Analyzing and Managing Remote Servers, Getting Help from Red Hat Customer Portal. Lab: Analyzing Servers and Getting Support.
NOTE — Lower exam priority than most chapters — and that's worth knowing, not hiding

The RHCSA exam is a hands-on, command-line practical test — it doesn't grade whether you can navigate a web portal. This chapter is mostly GUI tools (Web Console, the Customer Portal website, the Red Hat Insights dashboard), so treat it as real-world professional awareness rather than exam drilling. The one genuinely hands-on, testable piece is enabling the cockpit.socket service itself — that's an ordinary systemctl task straight out of Chapter 9.

sections.title: 16.1 Web Console (Cockpit) — a browser-based admin interface

content.text: Web Console is RHEL's built-in web management UI, built on the open source Cockpit project. It's installed by default on every install type except a Minimal Install — which is exactly the install type Part 0 of this guide used, so you'll need to install it yourself to actually try it.
sudo dnf install cockpit # only needed on a Minimal Install, like this guide's lab VMs
sudo systemctl enable --now cockpit.socket # exam-critical pattern from Chapter 9 — enable AND start in one line
sudo firewall-cmd --add-service=cockpit --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --reload

Once running, browse to https://servername:9090 and log in with any local account's username and password, including root. A self-signed TLS certificate is used out of the box, so your browser will show a security warning on first connection — expected on an unconfigured system, not a sign of compromise.
What you can do (privileged login)
Where
View real-time CPU/memory/disk/network graphs
System
Browse and filter systemd journal entries by date range and severity
Logs
Get a full interactive terminal, in the browser
Terminal
Start/stop/enable/disable services graphically
Services
Generate a diagnostic report (sosreport-style bundle) for a support case
Diagnostic Reports
Manage user accounts, including SSH keys and password resets
Accounts
Restart or shut down the system
System → Power Options
💡 Why this matters — Why this is worth knowing even though it's GUI

Everything Web Console does maps directly onto a command you already know from earlier chapters — its Services page is systemctl, its Terminal is just SSH in a browser tab, its Logs page is journalctl with a point-and-click filter. It's genuinely useful when you need a quick visual (a performance graph, a log filter) or when handing basic access to someone less comfortable at a command line — not a replacement for CLI fluency, which is what the exam actually tests.

access.redhat.com is where documentation, Knowledgebase articles, downloads, and support-case management live. Some content is public; deeper Knowledgebase solutions and case-filing require an active subscription — exactly the kind of entitlement you registered for back in Chapter 14/Part 0.
Portal area
What it's for
Subscriptions
Manage registered systems, entitlements, and activation keys
Downloads
Product ISOs, updates, evaluation entitlements
Support Cases
File and track support tickets (needs sufficient support-tier access)
Knowledgebase
Searchable solution articles, FAQs, troubleshooting guides
redhat-support-tool brings Knowledgebase search to the command line, useful specifically because it works without ever leaving an SSH session:
redhat-support-tool # opens an interactive prompt
# Command (? for help): search subscription-manager entitlements
# ...pick a result number to read it, q to back out

First use prompts for Customer Portal credentials and offers to save them locally (~/.redhat-support-tool/redhat-support-tool.conf, or system-wide with --global) so you're not re-entering them on every search.

sections.title: 16.3 Red Hat Insights — proactive, automated system analysis

content.text: Insights is a SaaS analytics service: a lightweight client uploads anonymized configuration metadata from your system, and Red Hat's rule engine checks it against a continuously updated set of known security, stability, performance, and availability issues — surfacing problems before they cause an outage, often with an auto-generated Ansible Playbook to fix them.
sudo dnf install insights-client
sudo insights-client --register # one-time registration, requires an active subscription entitlement
sudo insights-client # re-run any time to refresh the uploaded metadata
Results appear at access.redhat.com/insights, not on the local system — there's no local report to read; the analysis genuinely happens server-side.
Risk factor
Meaning
Likelihood
How likely this specific issue is to actually affect this system
Impact
How severe the consequences would be if it does
Total Risk
Likelihood × Impact, combined into one score
Risk of change
How disruptive the RECOMMENDED FIX itself might be to apply
💡 Why this matters — Why "risk of change" is tracked as its own separate number

A fix's own risk matters independently from the problem's risk — the book's own example is a kernel security issue that needs an update and reboot to fully resolve, but can be temporarily mitigated with a config change requiring no downtime at all. Knowing both numbers lets you apply the safe mitigation now and schedule the disruptive full fix for a proper maintenance window, rather than treating every recommendation as equally urgent to apply immediately.

The standard remediation loop: read the issue's "Steps to resolve" in the web UI, perform them on the actual system, then re-run insights-client to upload fresh metadata — the issue should then disappear from that system's list once the updated data confirms it's fixed.

sections.title: Hands-on: practice these on your own lab

content.text: 1. On workstation: sudo dnf install cockpit; sudo systemctl enable --now cockpit.socket; sudo firewall-cmd --add-service=cockpit --permanent && sudo firewall-cmd --reload.
2. From your host machine's browser, visit https://<workstation's IP>:9090, accept the self-signed cert warning, and log in as student.
3. In Web Console, open Logs and filter to the last hour — compare what you see against the equivalent journalctl --since "-1 hour" command from Chapter 11.
4. Open Terminal inside Web Console and run a command you already know (id, systemctl status sshd) — confirm it behaves exactly like a normal SSH session.
5. (Optional, requires a real Red Hat subscription entitlement) sudo insights-client --register on one lab VM, then check access.redhat.com/insights after a few minutes to see it appear.
1. Q1 — Why won't Web Console be running by default on the lab VMs built in Part 0 of this guide, even though it's installed by default on most RHEL 8 installs?
2. Q2 — What's the practical difference between Total Risk and Risk of change in a Red Hat Insights recommendation, and why might you act on a low-total-risk issue before a high-total-risk one?
NOTE — Answers

Q1 — Web Console is excluded specifically from Minimal Install, which is exactly the install type Part 0's lab build used — it has to be installed manually (dnf install cockpit) before it can be enabled.

Q2 — Total Risk scores how serious the underlying PROBLEM is; Risk of change scores how disruptive the RECOMMENDED FIX would be to apply. You might apply a low-total-risk fix immediately specifically because it's also low-risk-of-change (quick, safe, no downtime), while deferring a high-total-risk issue's fix to a scheduled maintenance window if fixing it is itself disruptive — the two numbers let you separate urgency from convenience of remediation.

Web Console (Cockpit) is a browser-based admin UI at https://host:9090, enabled with systemctl enable --now cockpit.socket — everything it does maps onto a CLI command you already know from earlier chapters.
The Red Hat Customer Portal (access.redhat.com) hosts documentation, Knowledgebase, downloads, and support cases; redhat-support-tool brings Knowledgebase search to the command line.

Red Hat Insights (insights-client) uploads anonymized config metadata for server-side analysis against known issues, scoring each by Likelihood, Impact, Total Risk, and separately, Risk of change for the fix itself.
This chapter is lower priority for direct exam prep than most others — it's professional context and a GUI toolset, not a set of hands-on tasks the RHCSA grades.
